title: Optical Spectra
short_intro: Optical spectra comprise discrete emission or absorption lines and bands in the ultraviolet, visible, and infrared regions arising from electronic transitions between atomic or molecular energy levels. These spectra provide fundamental insights into electronic configurations, coupling schemes, and fine structures of atoms.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic understanding of atomic excitation, emission, Bohr's frequency condition, hydrogen spectrum series (Lyman, Balmer, Paschen, Brackett, Pfund), and simple selection rules.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Detailed treatment of fine structure, spin-orbit interaction, L-S and j-j coupling schemes, Zeeman effect, Stark effect, Pauli's exclusion principle, and term symbols for multi-electron atoms.

concept_notes.heading: Origin of Optical Spectra
bullets: Optical spectra are produced when valence electrons undergo transitions between discrete electronic energy states accompanied by the emission or absorption of photons.
The frequency of the emitted radiation is given by Bohr's frequency condition: hν = E<sub>2</sub> - E<sub>1</sub>.
Spectra are classified into line spectra (atomic gases), band spectra (molecules), and continuous spectra (incandescent solids).

concept_notes.heading: Hydrogen Spectrum and Spectral Series
bullets: The atomic spectrum of hydrogen consists of distinct series of lines corresponding to transitions terminating at a specific lower principal quantum number n<sub>1</sub>.

Lyman series (n<sub>1</sub> = 1, UV region), Balmer series (n<sub>1</sub> = 2, Visible region), Paschen series (n<sub>1</sub> = 3, IR region), Brackett (n<sub>1</sub> = 4), and Pfund (n<sub>1</sub> = 5).
Wave numbers of these spectral lines are accurately predicted by the Rydberg formula using the reduced mass of the electron-proton system.

concept_notes.heading: Fine Structure and Coupling Schemes
bullets: High-resolution optical spectra reveal that single spectral lines split into closely spaced multiple components, known as fine structure, caused by spin-orbit interaction.

For lighter atoms, individual orbital angular momenta (L<sub>i</sub>) couple to form total orbital angular momentum L, and spin angular momenta (S<sub>i</sub>) couple to form total spin S (Russell-Saunders or L-S coupling).

For heavier atoms where spin-orbit interaction dominates over electrostatic repulsion between electrons, individual j<sub>i</sub> = l<sub>i</sub> + s<sub>i</sub> couple to form total J (j-j coupling).

concept_notes.heading: Selection Rules for Optical Transitions
bullets: Transitions between states are governed by quantum mechanical selection rules derived from parity and angular momentum conservation.
For single-electron atoms, the primary selection rules are Δl = ±1 and Δn = any integer.
For multi-electron systems under L-S coupling, the selection rules are ΔL = 0, ±1; ΔS = 0; ΔJ = 0, ±1 (with J = 0 to J = 0 forbidden).

derivations.title: Rydberg Formula for Hydrogen-like Atoms
derivations.conditions: Bohr's model with circular orbits and Coulomb electrostatic force providing centripetal acceleration, incorporating reduced mass μ.
steps: Write down the expression for total energy of an electron in the nth orbit: E<sub>n</sub> = -\frac{m e^4 Z^2}{8 \epsilon_0^2 h^2 n^2}.
Apply Bohr's frequency condition for a transition from upper state n<sub>2</sub> to lower state n<sub>1</sub>: \nu = \frac{E_{n_2} - E_{n_1}}{h}.
Substitute energy values and convert frequency to wave number \bar{\nu} = \frac{\nu}{c} = \frac{E_{n_2} - E_{n_1}}{hc}.
Express wave number in terms of Rydberg constant R<sub>∞</sub> = \frac{m e^4}{8 \epsilon_0^2 c h^3}.

derivations.title: Spin-Orbit Interaction Energy Shift
derivations.conditions: Perturbation theory approach to evaluate magnetic energy of electron spin in the magnetic field generated by orbital motion of the nucleus.
steps: Calculate the effective magnetic field B experienced by the electron in its rest frame due to the nuclear motion: B = \frac{1}{2m_0^2 c^2 r} \left( \frac{dV}{dr} \right) \vec{L}.
Determine the potential energy perturbation due to interaction between magnetic dipole moment μ<sub>s</sub> and magnetic field B: ΔE = -\vec{\mu}_s \cdot \vec{B}.
Substitute μ<sub>s</sub> = -\frac{e}{m_0}\vec{S} and take the expectation value over quantum states characterized by L, S, and J.
Express the resulting energy shift in terms of total angular momentum quantum numbers J, L, and S: E_{SO} = \frac{A}{2} [J(J+1) - L(L+1) - S(S+1)].

graphs_and_experiments.title: Grotrian Diagram (Energy Level Diagram)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Horizontal energy levels grouped by principal quantum number n and orbital angular momentum l, with vertical arrows indicating allowed optical transitions.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates permitted transitions, selection rules, and the branching ratios of atomic emission lines.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Directly tested in PGT exams to identify allowed vs forbidden transitions and term structures.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Hydrogen Emission Spectrum Series
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A logarithmic or linear wavelength scale showing converging spectral lines grouped into Lyman, Balmer, and Paschen series converging to distinct series limits.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the 1/n<sup>2</sup> dependence of energy levels and convergence to ionization potential at the series limit.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: TGT questions on identifying spectral regions (UV, Visible, IR) corresponding to specific series.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Normal Zeeman Effect Splitting
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Splitting of a single spectral line into three components (ν<sub>0</sub>, ν<sub>0</sub> ± Δν) when subjected to an external transverse or longitudinal magnetic field.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Direct proof of space quantization of angular momentum and magnetic moment associated with orbital motion.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual and numerical questions regarding frequency separation and polarization states.

solved_numericals.question: Find the shortest wavelength present in the Paschen series of hydrogen spectrum. (Given Rydberg constant R = 1.097 x 10^7 m^-1)
solution_steps: Identify the Paschen series lower state principal quantum number: n<sub>1</sub> = 3.
For the shortest wavelength (maximum energy transition), the upper state is n<sub>2</sub> = ∞.
Apply the Rydberg formula: 1/λ = R (1/n<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup> - 1/n<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup>) => 1/λ = 1.097 x 10^7 (1/3^2 - 1/∞^2).

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the Landé g-factor for a 2P3/2 state in L-S coupling.
solution_steps: Identify quantum numbers for 2P3/2 state: multiplicity = 2S+1 = 2, so S = 1/2.
Letter P corresponds to orbital quantum number L = 1.
Total angular momentum quantum number J = 3/2.
Substitute values into Landé g-factor formula: g = 1 + [J(J+1) + S(S+1) - L(L+1)] / [2J(J+1)].

solved_numericals.question: A spectral line of wavelength 589 nm undergoes Normal Zeeman effect in a magnetic field of 0.5 T. Calculate the wavelength shift (Δλ).
solution_steps: Frequency shift in Normal Zeeman effect is given by Δν = (e B) / (4 π m).
Substitute values: e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, B = 0.5 T, m = 9.1 x 10^-31 kg.
Relate wavelength shift to frequency shift: Δλ = (λ^2 / c) * Δν.
Substitute λ = 589 x 10^-9 m, c = 3 x 10^8 m/s, Δν = 6.99 x 10^9 Hz.

assumptions_and_limitations: Bohr-Sommerfeld model assumes non-relativistic electron velocities, which fails for inner-shell electrons in heavy elements where relativistic mass correction is mandatory.

Russell-Saunders (L-S) coupling assumes electrostatic interactions dominate over spin-orbit interactions, which breaks down for heavy atoms with high atomic number Z (where j-j coupling must be used).

common_misconceptions.wrong: All spectral series in hydrogen atom lie strictly within the visible region of the electromagnetic spectrum.
common_misconceptions.correct: Only the Balmer series lies partially in the visible region; Lyman is in the ultraviolet, and Paschen, Brackett, Pfund are in the infrared region.
common_misconceptions.why: The energy differences defining each series place them in entirely different electromagnetic wavelength bands.

common_misconceptions.wrong: In L-S coupling, individual electrons maintain independent spin and orbital angular momenta that do not interact with each other.
common_misconceptions.correct: Individual spin and orbital momenta couple vectorially to form resultant vectors L and S, which subsequently interact via spin-orbit coupling.
common_misconceptions.why: Electrostatic and magnetic interactions between electrons enforce collective coupling rather than isolated behavior.

quick_revision: Bohr's frequency condition equates photon energy to energy level differences: hν = ΔE.
The Rydberg formula calculates wave numbers of hydrogen spectral lines using principal quantum numbers.
Russell-Saunders coupling combines individual l<sub>i</sub> and s<sub>i</sub> into L and S before forming J = L + S.
Landé g-factor determines the magnetic splitting behavior of multi-electron atomic states in weak magnetic fields.
